steps.label: Do Now: Data Types (1 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: Data Types (1 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a program check the data type when a value is stored, and not later?Show the answer

The wrong kind of value would cause problems in every line that uses it. Stopping at once shows exactly where it went in.

From 2.2: data types. The program stops with an error.

1  DECLARE Name : STRING
2  DECLARE Height : INTEGER
3  DECLARE Paid : BOOLEAN
4  Name <- "Nok"
5  Height <- 1.47
6  Paid <- TRUE
7  OUTPUT Name
Total: 2 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: the wrong data type

steps.text: This is a different program. Do the same steps with your program.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Town : STRING
DECLARE Lives : STRING
Town <- "Songkhla"
Lives <- 3
OUTPUT Town

steps.text: DECLARE does not store anything. It only gives each variable its data type.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Town : STRING
DECLARE Lives : STRING
Town <- "Songkhla"
Lives <- 3
OUTPUT Town

steps.text: Line 3 stores "Songkhla" in Town. It is in quotes, so it is text. Town is a STRING, so that is fine.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Town : STRING
DECLARE Lives : STRING
Town <- "Songkhla"
Lives <- 3
OUTPUT Town

steps.text: Line 4 stores 3 in Lives. 3 has no quotes: it is a whole number. Lives was declared as a STRING, so the program stops here, on line 4.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Town : STRING
DECLARE Lives : STRING
Town <- "Songkhla"
Lives <- 3
OUTPUT Town
Lives <- 3: stops here

steps.text: The fix goes on the DECLARE line. A whole number needs INTEGER, so line 2 becomes DECLARE Lives : INTEGER. Now do yours.
steps.visual:
DECLARE Town : STRING
DECLARE Lives : STRING
Town <- "Songkhla"
Lives <- 3
OUTPUT Town

steps.label: Do Now: DIV, MOD and a Constant (2 of 2)
steps.content:
Do Now: DIV, MOD and a Constant (2 of 2)

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is the team size a constant and not a variable?Show the answer

It is set once and the program never needs to change it while it runs.

From 2.1 and 2.2. 30 is typed in.

1  CONSTANT TeamSize <- 4
2  DECLARE Pupils : INTEGER
3  INPUT Pupils
4  OUTPUT DIV(Pupils, TeamSize)
5  OUTPUT MOD(Pupils, TeamSize)
Total: 3 marks

walkthrough.title: Walk me through it: DIV, MOD and a constant

steps.text: This is a different program. 27 is typed in. Do the same steps with your program.
steps.visual:
CONSTANT BoxSize <- 6
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, BoxSize)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, BoxSize)

steps.text: BoxSize is a constant: it is 6 on every line that uses it.
steps.visual:
CONSTANT BoxSize <- 6
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, BoxSize)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, BoxSize)
BoxSize = 6

steps.text: DIV gives the whole number of times. 6 x 4 = 24, and 6 x 5 = 30 is too many.
steps.visual:
CONSTANT BoxSize <- 6
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, BoxSize)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, BoxSize)
DIV(27, 6) = 4

steps.text: MOD gives what is left over: 27 - 24 = 3.
steps.visual:
CONSTANT BoxSize <- 6
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, BoxSize)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, BoxSize)
MOD(27, 6) = 3

steps.text: Now line 1 is changed to 8. Every line that uses BoxSize uses 8 now. 8 x 3 = 24, so MOD(27, 8) is 27 - 24 = 3. Now do yours.
steps.visual:
CONSTANT BoxSize <- 8
DECLARE Eggs : INTEGER
INPUT Eggs
OUTPUT DIV(Eggs, BoxSize)
OUTPUT MOD(Eggs, BoxSize)

steps.label: 2.3: Conditional Statements
steps.content:
Programming, Logic and Testing

2.3: Conditional Statements

Year 8

  • Today: write programs that choose what to do, predict which lines run, and test that they choose right.
  • The big question: how does a program decide, and how do we know it decides correctly?
Think → Pair → ShareA lift door opens when a button is pressed. A game says "Game over" when lives run out. How can a program do different things at different times?Show the answer

It asks a question about a value, like "Are the lives 0?". The answer decides which lines run.

steps.label: What Is a Condition?
steps.content:
What Is a Condition?

Think → Pair → SharePredict: 12 is typed in. What is output? Why does the other OUTPUT line never run?Show the worked answer

Not yet.

Why? 12 >= 13 is FALSE, so the program jumps to ELSE. Only one of the two branches runs each time.

A condition is a question with only two answers: TRUE or FALSE.

1  DECLARE Age : INTEGER
2  INPUT Age
3  IF Age >= 13 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Join the club"
5  ELSE
6      OUTPUT "Not yet"
7  ENDIF
  • Line 3 holds the condition: Age >= 13.
  • TRUE: the THEN branch runs (line 4).
  • FALSE: the ELSE branch runs (line 6).
  • A branch is the lines for one answer. Only one branch runs.

steps.label: Six Comparison Operators
steps.content:
Six Comparison Operators

Think → Pair → ShareScore is 10. Why is Score > 10 FALSE, but Score >= 10 TRUE?Show the answer

10 is not more than 10. But 10 is equal to 10, and >= lets in "equal to" as well. One symbol changes the answer for that exact number.

A comparison operator compares two values. Here Score is 10.

OperatorMeaningExampleAnswer
=is equal toScore = 10TRUE
<>is not equal toScore <> 10FALSE
<is less thanScore < 10FALSE
<=is less than or equal toScore <= 10TRUE
>is more thanScore > 10FALSE
>=is more than or equal toScore >= 10TRUE

steps.label: Your Turn: TRUE or FALSE?
steps.content:
Your Turn: TRUE or FALSE?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy write the value of Coins into each condition before you decide?Show the answer

Then you compare two numbers you can see, and nothing is kept only in your head.

Coins is 7. Type TRUE or FALSE for each condition.

Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Compare: > and >=
steps.content:
Compare: > and >=

Think → Pair → SharePredict: 13 is typed into both programs. Which one lets the pupil join? Which program follows the rule?Show the worked answer

A outputs Not yet. B outputs Join the club.

Why? 13 > 13 is FALSE, but 13 >= 13 is TRUE. The rule says 13 or older, so B is right. For 12 or 14 the two programs give the same answer. Only 13 shows the difference.

The rule: pupils aged 13 or older can join the club.

A

DECLARE Age : INTEGER
INPUT Age
IF Age > 13 THEN
    OUTPUT "Join the club"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Not yet"
ENDIF

B

DECLARE Age : INTEGER
INPUT Age
IF Age >= 13 THEN
    OUTPUT "Join the club"
ELSE
    OUTPUT "Not yet"
ENDIF

steps.label: Predict: Which Branch Runs?
steps.content:
Predict: Which Branch Runs?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy put the typed value into the IF line before you choose?Show the answer

The IF line is where the program decides. Your answer depends on what that line gives.

Read each program. Choose the output. The answer shows after you choose.

A

1  DECLARE Mark : INTEGER
2  INPUT Mark
3  IF Mark > 50 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Pass"
5  ELSE
6      OUTPUT "Fail"
7  ENDIF

B

1  DECLARE Speed : INTEGER
2  INPUT Speed
3  IF Speed <= 90 THEN
4      OUTPUT "OK"
5  ELSE
6      OUTPUT "Too fast"
7  ENDIF

items.prompt: Program A: 50 is typed in. What is output?
items.explain: 50 > 50 is FALSE: 50 is not more than itself. So the ELSE branch runs.

items.prompt: Program B: 90 is typed in. What is output?
items.explain: 90 <= 90 is TRUE: <= lets in "equal to". So the THEN branch runs.

steps.label: Three Outcomes: An IF Inside an IF
steps.content:
Three Outcomes: An IF Inside an IF

Think → Pair → SharePredict: 65 is typed in. Which line is output? Why does line 6 get checked at all?Show the worked answer

Silver.

Why? 65 >= 80 is FALSE, so the program goes to the ELSE branch. The ELSE branch holds a second IF. 65 >= 50 is TRUE, so Silver is output.

One IF has two branches. For three outcomes, put a second IF inside the ELSE. This is a nested IF.

1  DECLARE Score : INTEGER
2  INPUT Score
3  IF Score >= 80 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Gold"
5  ELSE
6      IF Score >= 50 THEN
7          OUTPUT "Silver"
8      ELSE
9          OUTPUT "Bronze"
10      ENDIF
11  ENDIF
  • 80 or more: Gold.
  • 50 to 79: Silver.
  • Under 50: Bronze.
  • Each IF needs its own ENDIF.

steps.label: Watch the Program Choose
steps.content:
Watch the Program Choose

Think → Pair → ShareWhy say the next line out loud before you press Next?Show the answer

Predicting first shows you if you really know the rule. A wrong prediction tells you what to look at again.

Press Next step. Before each press, say which line runs next.

steps.label: Explain It: Why Only Gold?
steps.content:
Explain It: Why Only Gold?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is it useful to trace a program with your finger, one line at a time?Show the answer

You see each line the computer really reaches, in order, and you do not guess.

DECLARE Score : INTEGER
INPUT Score
IF Score >= 80 THEN
    OUTPUT "Gold"
ELSE
    IF Score >= 50 THEN
        OUTPUT "Silver"
    ELSE
        OUTPUT "Bronze"
    ENDIF
ENDIF

Explain it in your own words. Press Check my answer to have it marked.

items.context: Year 8 pseudocode lesson on IF statements. The program is the nested IF: IF Score >= 80 THEN OUTPUT "Gold" ELSE (IF Score >= 50 THEN OUTPUT "Silver" ELSE OUTPUT "Bronze" ENDIF) ENDIF. The class watched 85, 65 and 30 traced through it line by line. 85 is typed in. 85 is also 50 or more. Explain why the program outputs Gold only, and not Silver as well.
items.prompt: 85 is typed in. 85 is also 50 or more. Explain why the program outputs Gold only, and not Silver as well.
items.modelAnswer: 85 >= 80 is TRUE, so the THEN branch runs and outputs Gold (1). The ELSE branch is skipped, so the Score >= 50 check is never made (1).
scheme: The first condition (Score >= 80 / 85 >= 80) is TRUE, so the THEN branch runs / Gold is output
The ELSE branch is skipped / the second IF (Score >= 50) is never checked / only one branch runs
items.guidance: Credit the idea in the student's own words. Point 2 needs the idea that the second check is skipped or not reached; "only one branch runs" alone earns it. Do not award point 2 for just restating that Gold is output.

steps.label: Compare: Which IF Comes First?
steps.content:
Compare: Which IF Comes First?

Think → Pair → SharePredict: 85 is typed into both. What does each one output? Can A ever output Gold?Show the worked answer

A outputs Silver. B outputs Gold.

Why? In A, 85 >= 50 is TRUE first, so the ELSE branch, with the Gold check, is skipped. Every score of 80 or more is also 50 or more, so A can never output Gold. Check the biggest group first.

Same rule: 80 or more is Gold, 50 or more is Silver. The checks are in a different order.

A: 50 first

DECLARE Score : INTEGER
INPUT Score
IF Score >= 50 THEN
    OUTPUT "Silver"
ELSE
    IF Score >= 80 THEN
        OUTPUT "Gold"
    ELSE
        OUTPUT "Bronze"
    ENDIF
ENDIF

B: 80 first

DECLARE Score : INTEGER
INPUT Score
IF Score >= 80 THEN
    OUTPUT "Gold"
ELSE
    IF Score >= 50 THEN
        OUTPUT "Silver"
    ELSE
        OUTPUT "Bronze"
    ENDIF
ENDIF

steps.label: Your Turn: Check the Order
steps.content:
Your Turn: Check the Order

Think → Pair → ShareWhy read the rule above the program before you trace it?Show the answer

The rule says what should happen. The trace shows what does happen. You need both to spot a mistake.

The rule: 30 or more is Hot, 20 to 29 is Warm, under 20 is Cold.

1  DECLARE Temp : INTEGER
2  INPUT Temp
3  IF Temp >= 20 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Warm"
5  ELSE
6      IF Temp >= 30 THEN
7          OUTPUT "Hot"
8      ELSE
9          OUTPUT "Cold"
10      ENDIF
11  ENDIF
Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Explain It: Why Check 80 First?
steps.content:
Explain It: Why Check 80 First?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy say your explanation to a partner before you type it?Show the answer

Saying it out loud shows the gaps. Your partner can ask what you mean.

Explain it in your own words. Press Check my answer to have it marked.

items.context: Year 8 pseudocode lesson on nested IF statements. Program A checked Score >= 50 first and Score >= 80 inside its ELSE, so 85 gave Silver and Gold was never output. Program B checked Score >= 80 first and gave Gold. Explain why the Score >= 80 check must come before the Score >= 50 check.
items.prompt: Explain why the Score >= 80 check must come before the Score >= 50 check.
items.modelAnswer: A score of 80 or more is also 50 or more, so if the 50 check came first it would be TRUE (1). Then the ELSE branch with the 80 check is skipped, so Gold would never be output (1).
scheme: A score of 80 or more is also 50 or more / the >= 50 condition is TRUE for high scores too
So the 80 check would be skipped / never reached, and Gold would never be output / high scores get Silver
items.guidance: Credit the idea in the student's own words, with any example score of 80 or more. Point 2 follows on from point 1.

steps.label: Activity 1: Which Branch Runs?
steps.content:
Activity 1: Which Branch Runs?

Think → Pair → ShareWhy predict first, then check?Show the answer

A wrong prediction shows you which rule to look at again.

Predict each answer, then check. The programs and values change every time, and they get harder: TRUE or FALSE, one IF, a nested IF, then choose the operator.

steps.label: Activity: PyScratch Task 1
steps.content:
Activity: PyScratch Task 1 of 3

Think → Pair → ShareWhy type in more than one value when you test your fix?Show the answer

A fix for one value can break another. Each value tries a different part of the program.

What to do: fix or write the program in the box on the left. Click the green flag above the stage to run it. When it works, click Check my program. Task 1 of 3: fix one line.

steps.label: Test Every Branch
steps.content:
Test Every Branch

Think → Pair → ShareSam tested 30 and 70, and both outputs were right. He says the program works. Is he right? Which age would you test?Show the worked answer

No. Type 65: the program outputs 100, but the rule says 40.

Why? 65 > 65 is FALSE. The IF line should use >=. Sam tested each branch once, but not the number written in the condition, where > and >= give different answers.

The rule: a cinema ticket costs 40 baht for people aged 65 or older, and 100 baht for everyone else.

1  DECLARE Age : INTEGER
2  INPUT Age
3  IF Age > 65 THEN
4      OUTPUT 40
5  ELSE
6      OUTPUT 100
7  ENDIF
Age typedExpectedOutput
30100100
704040
  • Test one value for each branch.
  • Also test the number in the condition itself.
  • Write the expected output before you run it.
  • A test passes only if the output matches.

steps.label: Your Turn: Find the Test That Fails
steps.content:
Your Turn: Find the Test That Fails

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does a tester write down the expected output before running the program?Show the answer

So the real output can be compared with it. Without it, a wrong output can look fine.

The rule: a bag of 20 kg or more must pay extra. Lighter bags are free. Weights are whole numbers.

1  DECLARE Weight : INTEGER
2  INPUT Weight
3  IF Weight > 20 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Pay extra"
5  ELSE
6      OUTPUT "Free"
7  ENDIF
Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Activity 2: Write the IF
steps.content:
Activity 2: Write the IF

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does the drill type in new values every time?Show the answer

A program must work for any value it is given, not just one.

Write each program from the rule. New values are typed in every time, often the number in the condition, so > and >= matter.

steps.label: Activity: PyScratch Task 2
steps.content:
Activity: PyScratch Task 2 of 3

Think → Pair → ShareWhy is the program still right for a score of 60 after your change?Show the answer

Your change must only add a new outcome. The old ones must still work the same way.

Task 2 of 3: change a program that already works.

steps.label: Activity: PyScratch Task 3
steps.content:
Activity: PyScratch Task 3 of 3

Think → Pair → ShareWhy does Check my program change Limit and run your program again?Show the answer

If the result changes too, the IF really uses the constant. A number typed into the IF would not change.

Task 3 of 3: write the whole program yourself.

steps.label: Practice: Find and Fix
steps.content:
Practice: Find and Fix

Think → Pair → ShareWhy can a program have no error message and still be wrong?Show the answer

The computer runs what is written, not what the programmer meant.

The rule: 90 or more gets a Star, 60 to 89 gets a Tick, under 60 gets Keep going.

1  DECLARE Mark : INTEGER
2  INPUT Mark
3  IF Mark >= 60 THEN
4      OUTPUT "Tick"
5  ELSE
6      IF Mark > 90 THEN
7          OUTPUT "Star"
8      ELSE
9          OUTPUT "Keep going"
10      ENDIF
11  ENDIF
Total: 3 marks

steps.label: Circuit Siege: How to Play
steps.content:
Circuit Siege: How to Play

Think → Pair → ShareWhy do the questions come between the waves?Show the answer

You need coins for towers, and right answers earn them. Thinking well keeps your base safe.

  1. Build towers on the path.
  2. Stop the bugs before they reach your base.
  3. Between waves, answer questions from 2.1 and 2.2 to earn coins: data types, constants and library functions. Some have an IF to trace.

steps.label: Play: Circuit Siege
steps.content:
Play: Circuit Siege

Think → Pair → ShareWhy read the whole program before you answer?Show the answer

One line at the top, like a DECLARE or a CONSTANT, changes what every later line can do.

steps.label: Plenary: Conditional Statements
steps.content:
Plenary: Conditional Statements

Think → Pair → ShareWhy practise with new values every time?Show the answer

If you can trace any value, you really know how the IF chooses.

Conditions, which branch runs, nested IFs, the order of the checks, and testing. Your progress is saved.
